theme: Eliphaz concludes; Job replies, the cry of the afflicted soul
readingInstruction: Read Job 5:1-7:21. Eliphaz finishes his speech in chapter 5, and Job answers in chapters 6 and 7. Notice the turn in chapter 7, when Job stops speaking to his friends and begins speaking to God.
settingTheScene: Yesterday Eliphaz began his speech with a general rule. Today he finishes it. His tone moves from correction to advice, and he gives Job a plan: seek God, accept discipline, and everything will be restored. He means well. But a plan of recovery assumes that Job did something wrong. Job’s reply is the first long speech where he speaks both to his friends and to God, and it is one of the rawest passages in Scripture.
observation: Eliphaz says, “Man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward” (5:7).
He advises, “As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause” (5:8).
He describes God as one who “does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number” (5:9) and who lifts the lowly (5:11).
He says, “Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty” (5:17).
Job answers, “Oh that my vexation were weighed” (6:2), and says his words have been rash because of his pain.
Job compares his friends to a seasonal stream that dries up in the heat when travelers need it (6:15-21).
He asks, “Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray” (6:24).
In chapter 7 he says, “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle” (7:6) and “I will not restrain my mouth” (7:11).
He asks God, “What is man, that you make so much of him…that you visit him every morning and test him every moment?” (7:17-18).
interpretation:
Eliphaz sounds wise because much of what he says is true. God does lift up the lowly. God does discipline those he loves. Later the writer of Hebrews will quote Proverbs about this very thing (Hebrews 12:5-6). The problem is that Eliphaz applies it to Job without knowing anything about Job’s case. The truth is real, and the application is wrong. That is one of the hardest things to learn about reading and using Scripture: a true statement can be false in a particular place.

Job’s reply begins with a plea for understanding. “Oh that my vexation were weighed.” He is not asking his friends to agree with him. He is asking them to see the weight of what he carries. And he makes an honest complaint about their help. They are like a wadi in the desert, running with water in the winter and gone in the heat. When a traveler most needs water, there is none. A friend’s faithfulness is measured in the dry season.

Then he makes a request that is entirely fair. “Teach me, and I will be silent.” He is open to correction. “How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove?” (6:25). If they can show him a sin, he will listen. They cannot, because there is none to show.

Chapter 7 is where the speech changes direction. Job stops talking about his friends and begins talking to God. His language is bitter. He sees life as hard service and hired labor, he cannot sleep, and his skin is breaking. He asks God, “Am I the sea, or the sea monster, that you set a guard over me?” (7:12). He even parodies Psalm 8. Where David asked in wonder, “What is man that you are mindful of him?”, Job asks in pain what man is that God cannot leave him alone.

Do not read this as rebellion. Notice that Job is still speaking to God. The friends talk about God, and Job talks to him. That difference is the whole difference between theology as theory and faith as a relationship, and it is the reason God will say later that Job spoke rightly.
connection: Hebrews 12:5-11 quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 on discipline, and it is meant for children who are being trained, not for people who are suffering unjustly. Psalm 8 is the passage Job twists in 7:17-18, and Hebrews 2:5-9 reads Psalm 8 as fulfilled in Jesus. Psalm 88 will show you another prayer that does not end with comfort.
application:
When you read the Bible to comfort or counsel someone, ask whether the verse fits their situation, or whether you are using it to solve your own discomfort with their pain.

When you are the one in pain, pray as Job did. Speak to God, not only about him. If your prayers sound bitter, take them to the one person who can bear them.

Think of a person who was a seasonal stream for you, and one who was a river. Aim to be the second.
prayerPrompts: Bring your complaints to God and not around him.
Ask him to make you a faithful friend in someone’s dry season.
Ask for wisdom to speak truth with love.
